headline: Little Egg reshapes on the moving sand — peanut bunker pull the first bonito, fluke slide off the bar
subhead: The inlet cut is throwing new structure just as peanut schools show, and the back bay doormats are already gone to the ocean side.
body_markdown:
The sandbar off the south end of Holgate has moved again. Anyone who's run a drone over that stretch in the last ten days can see it — the outer bar that held through most of August has slid west and pinched down, and there's a new gut forming on the inside edge that's dumping current straight into the wash on the back half of the ebb. That kind of reshuffle usually means one thing this time of year: it's grabbing peanut bunker and holding them against the beach, and that's exactly what showed up this week.

We flagged this last week — said with bonito and albies already working the coast north and south of LBI, this stretch was a good bet to light up within the week — and that's more or less how it played out. Scattered false albacore and a few bonito have been showing in the wash off Holgate and around the Little Egg Inlet rip on the last two hours of the outgoing, chasing peanut bunker that are getting pushed and squeezed by the new structure. It's not a blitz yet. It's flashes — a school comes through on the moving current, blows up for five or ten minutes, then goes quiet. Anyone throwing small — half-ounce Deadly Dicks, Hogy epoxy jigs, or 3-inch Albie Snax on light spinning gear — has had shots. The window is tight and it's tide-dependent: the last two hours of the ebb through the start of the new flood at Little Egg has been the best of it, when the current is ripping hardest through that reshaped cut.

Bluefish are the more dependable player right now. They're mixing right into those same peanut bunker schools at the inlet mouth and along the Barnegat Light jetty rocks, and they'll eat almost anything metal — Ava jigs, Kastmasters, tin squids — worked through the rip on a moving tide. That consistency tracks with what's been happening basin-wide; warm water has kept blues aggressive and spread out all summer, and there's no sign of that changing before Labor Day weekend closes out.

Fluke is the other half of the story, and it's not a good-news half. Back bay fluke fishing on this stretch — Great Bay, the Mullica flats, the deeper holes off Graveling Point — is thinning out fast, right on the seasonal schedule. Water in the back is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, warm enough that the bigger fish have already started sliding out through Little Egg Inlet toward ocean-side structure. If you want a shot at a quality doormat right now, the better play is the deeper edges outside the inlet — the humps and hard bottom off Beach Haven and the drop-offs along the outer bar — rather than the bay itself. Bucktails tipped with Gulp in white or chartreuse, dragged slow along bottom in 20 to 35 feet, are still producing, but the numbers game inside the bay is over for the season.

Striped bass are the fish everyone's asking about, and the honest answer is: not yet, but soon. Bunker schools are stacking up in the bigger staging areas to our north — Raritan Bay, the south shore beaches, up into Narragansett Bay — and that's the trigger everyone's watching. Locally, there's bass mixed in around bait pods staged off the inlet and in the deeper channel edges of Little Egg, but they're not committing to blitz behavior. Water's still carrying enough late-summer warmth to keep them scattered and non-committal rather than stacked and aggressive. The moon builds toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should tighten tidal flow and start squeezing those loose bait schools into something more concentrated. That's usually the ingredient that flips the switch. If the first real cool front of the season lines up with that tide push in the next week to ten days, expect the first legitimate blitz activity to break — and when it does on this stretch, it'll likely start in the surf at Holgate and the deeper edges of Little Egg Inlet before it shows up anywhere in the back bay.

Worth watching alongside all of this: the finger mullet are starting to stage in the back creeks off the Mullica and around Graveling Point, which is the first real marker of the fall mullet run building. It's early — the heavy push usually doesn't show until the back half of September — but the bait's there, and once it starts moving out through Little Egg on the outgoing tides, that's historically when the bass bite in the surf really turns over for real. Rig accordingly: keep a bag with peanut bunker imitations for the albie/bonito window, tins for the blues, and start setting aside some bunker-profile swimmers and darters for when that mullet push gets underway.

If there's only one tide to fish this weekend, make it the last two hours of the ebb into the first hour of flood at Little Egg Inlet — that's where the new cut is concentrating bait, and it's the window that's produced the most consistent action on bonito, albies, and blues alike. Keep the plug bag light and organized, because these are fast-moving, tide-triggered windows, not all-day soaks.
